subject: Chemistry
title: Personalized Medicine: Your DNA, Your Drug
description: A quick, practical guide to Personalized Medicine: Your DNA, Your Drug.

hook.text: The same drug can cure one person and kill another. Personalized medicine uses your genetics to pick the right treatment.

buildup.text: Pharmacogenomics studies how genes affect drug response. CYP enzymes in your liver metabolize most drugs—but variants differ.

discovery.text: Some people metabolize codeine too fast, creating dangerous morphine levels. Others metabolize it too slowly, getting no relief.

twist.text: The FDA now requires genetic testing for over 300 drugs. A simple cheek swab can predict which medicines will work for you.

climax.text: Whole genome sequencing costs under $200 today. In the future, every prescription could be tailored to your DNA.

punchline.text: Same drug, different genes, different outcomes. Your DNA decides how medicine works.

quiz.question: Why can the same drug dose be dangerous for one person but ineffective for another?
options: Genetic variants in liver enzymes cause people to metabolize drugs at different rates
People develop random allergies to different drug ingredients
Age is the only factor that determines drug effectiveness

details.summary: Personalized medicine uses genetic information to predict how individuals will respond to specific drugs, allowing physicians to select the most effective treatment with the fewest side effects..
details.whyItMatters: Adverse drug reactions kill over 100,000 people annually in the US alone. Pharmacogenomics can prevent many of these deaths by matching drugs to individual genetic profiles before prescribing.
takeaways: Genetic variants affect how quickly individuals metabolize specific drugs
CYP2D6 enzyme variants alone affect the metabolism of 25 percent of all drugs
Pharmacogenomic testing can prevent dangerous adverse drug reactions

faq.question: Why do the same drugs work differently in different people?
faq.answer: Genetic variations in drug-metabolizing enzymes, transport proteins, and drug targets cause different rates of drug activation, breakdown, and response. A person with fast CYP2D6 metabolism may clear a drug too quickly for it to work, while a slow metabolizer may accumulate toxic levels.

faq.question: How widespread is pharmacogenomic testing in clinical practice currently?
faq.answer: Adoption is growing but remains uneven. The FDA has pharmacogenomic information on over 300 drug labels. Some hospitals routinely test for specific variants before prescribing drugs like warfarin or clopidogrel..
